interactions.label: A patient with heart failure reports worsening breathlessness whenever he lies f

params.question: A patient with heart failure reports worsening breathlessness whenever he lies flat and needs to prop himself up on several pillows to sleep. This symptom is best explained by:

answers.text: Reduced cardiac output causing skeletal muscle hypoperfusion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Reduced cardiac output causes fatigue and exercise intolerance (forward failure), not positional breathlessness.

answers.text: Increased venous return in the supine position raising pulmonary capillary pressure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Lying flat redistributes blood from the lower limbs into the central circulation, increasing pulmonary venous pressure and causing fluid transudation into the alveoli — a classic left-sided backward failure mechanism.

answers.text: Elevated systemic venous pressure causing hepatic congestion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hepatic congestion results from right-sided backward failure and presents as hepatomegaly and right upper quadrant discomfort, not orthopnoea.

answers.text: Nocturnal reabsorption of peripheral oedema fluid causing increased urine output

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Nocturnal reabsorption of oedema fluid explains nocturia (increased night-time urination), a forward failure phenomenon, not positional breathlessness.

overallFeedback.feedback: Orthopnoea results from left-sided backward failure. Lying flat increases venous return, raising pulmonary capillary pressure and causing pulmonary congestion — that is why heart failure patients sleep propped up on pillows.
Exactly right. Orthopnoea is a hallmark of left-sided backward failure — the supine position increases venous return, raises pulmonary capillary pressure, and drives fluid into the lungs.

interactions.label: The most common cause of isolated right heart failure is cor pulmonale from chro

params.question: The most common cause of isolated right heart failure is cor pulmonale from chronic lung disease.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is true. While left heart failure is the most common cause of right heart failure overall, it causes biventricular failure, not isolated right-sided disease. Cor pulmonale from chronic lung disease is the single most important cause of isolated right heart failure.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Cor pulmonale — right ventricular failure driven by chronic lung disease — is the leading cause of isolated right heart failure. Left heart failure is the most common cause of right heart failure overall, but it produces biventricular failure rather than isolated right-sided disease.

params.question: A patient with heart failure and an ejection fraction of 28% has an ECG showing a QRS duration of 160 ms with broad, notched R waves in leads I, aVL, V5, and V6. This pattern is most clinically significant because it:

answers.text: Confirms a prior myocardial infarction as the cause of heart failure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pathological Q waves indicate a prior myocardial infarction, not left bundle branch block. LBBB widens the QRS and alters R-wave morphology but does not produce Q waves.
Atrial fibrillation is identified by an irregularly irregular rhythm with absent P waves — a rhythm diagnosis, not a QRS morphology finding. This tracing describes left bundle branch block.

answers.text: Identifies a potential candidate for cardiac resynchronisation therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Left bundle branch block with a widened QRS combined with reduced ejection fraction is the key criterion for considering cardiac resynchronisation therapy, which can improve ventricular coordination and outcomes.

answers.text: Suggests right ventricular strain from pulmonary hypertension

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Right ventricular strain typically produces right axis deviation and ST-T changes in the right-sided leads (V1–V3), not broad notched R waves in the lateral leads.

overallFeedback.feedback: This ECG pattern describes left bundle branch block. When found in a patient with reduced ejection fraction, LBBB is the key indicator for considering cardiac resynchronisation therapy.
Well analysed. LBBB with a widened QRS and reduced ejection fraction is the trigger for considering cardiac resynchronisation therapy — recognising this pattern directly changes management.

params.question: A 65-year-old patient with heart failure and ejection fraction of 35% is on optimal doses of sacubitril/valsartan, carvedilol, spironolactone, and dapagliflozin, yet remains breathless with ankle oedema. Which additional drug would best relieve his congestion?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: An ACE inhibitor must never be combined with ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) because of the increased risk of life-threatening angioedema. This patient is already on ARNI.
The patient is already taking carvedilol, one of the three evidence-based beta-blockers for heart failure. Adding a second beta-blocker is not appropriate.
The patient is already on dapagliflozin, an SGLT2 inhibitor. Adding a second agent from the same class provides no additional benefit.

Correct. Loop diuretics like furosemide relieve congestion and reduce oedema. They do not improve survival, but they are essential for symptom control when a patient remains congested despite all four pillars of guideline-directed therapy.

overallFeedback.feedback: This patient is already on all four mortality-reducing pillars (ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor). For persistent congestion, the next step is a loop diuretic such as furosemide — it relieves symptoms even though it does not improve survival.

Spot on. With all four mortality-reducing pillars already optimised, a loop diuretic is the right addition for persistent congestion — remember that diuretics control symptoms but do not reduce mortality.

interactions.label: A 20-year-old woman is found to have fixed splitting of the second heart sound o

params.question: A 20-year-old woman is found to have fixed splitting of the second heart sound on auscultation. Echocardiography confirms a left-to-right shunt. This presentation is most consistent with:

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Fixed splitting of S2 is the hallmark of atrial septal defect — the constant left-to-right shunt maintains elevated right ventricular volume throughout the respiratory cycle, preventing the normal variation in splitting.
A ventricular septal defect produces a harsh pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, not fixed splitting of the second heart sound.
Patent ductus arteriosus produces a continuous machinery murmur because the pressure gradient across the ductus persists throughout the cardiac cycle, not fixed splitting of S2.
Tetralogy of Fallot is a cyanotic congenital heart disease with right-to-left shunting. It would present with cyanosis and clubbing, not an isolated finding of fixed split S2 with left-to-right flow.

overallFeedback.feedback: Fixed splitting of the second heart sound is the hallmark auscultatory finding of atrial septal defect, an acyanotic lesion where the constant left-to-right shunt maintains elevated right ventricular volume throughout the respiratory cycle.

Exactly right. Fixed splitting of S2 is the signature finding of ASD — the constant left-to-right shunt keeps right ventricular volume elevated regardless of respiration, eliminating the normal splitting variation.
